butir.teks: Clarification of the deception in likening these debates to the consultations of the Companions and the discussions of the early generations (salaf)

Know that these people may lure others into this by saying: our aim in debates is to investigate the truth so that it becomes clear, for the truth is sought, and cooperation in examining knowledge and the convergence of thoughts is beneficial and effective. Such was the custom of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) in their consultations, like their consultation on the question of the grandfather and the brothers, the fixed penalty (hadd) for drinking wine, and the obligation of the imam to pay compensation when he errs, as is reported in the case of the woman who miscarried her fetus out of fear of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and as is reported of questions of the shares of inheritance and others, and what is reported from al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, Malik, Abu Yusuf, and others among the scholars (may Allah Most High have mercy on them).

What I am about to mention will make you aware of this deception: cooperation in seeking the truth is part of the religion, but it has eight conditions and signs. The first is that he does not engage in it, it being one of

the communal obligations (fard kifaya), while he has not freed himself from the individual obligations. Whoever has an individual obligation upon him and engages in a communal obligation and claims that his aim is the truth is a liar.

An example is one who neglects the prayer in his own case and devotes himself to obtaining garments and weaving them, saying: my aim is to cover the nakedness of one who prays naked and finds no garment, for that may happen and its occurrence is possible, just as the jurist claims that the occurrence of the rare cases that the inquiry in juristic disagreement is about is possible.

Those who engage in debate neglect matters that are individual obligations by agreement. Whoever is required to return a deposit at once, yet gets up and begins the prayer, which is the closest of the acts of drawing near to Allah Most High, disobeys by it. So it is not enough, for a person to be obedient, that his act is of the kind of acts of obedience, unless the time, the conditions, and the order are observed in it.

The second is that he does not see a communal obligation more important than debate. If he sees what is more important and does something else, he disobeys by his act. His example is that of one who sees a group of thirsty people on the verge of perishing, whom the people have neglected, while he is able to keep them alive by giving them water to drink, but he busies himself with learning cupping (hijama) and claims that it is one of the communal obligations, and that if the city were without it the people would perish. When it is said to him, "In the city there is a group of cuppers, and in them is sufficiency," he says, "This does not take this act out of being a communal obligation."

So the case of one who does this and neglects attending to the calamity that has befallen a group of thirsty Muslims is like the case of one who engages in debate while in the city there are neglected communal obligations that no one carries out. As for the legal opinion (fatwa), a group has taken it up. No city is free of a number of neglected obligations, and the jurists pay no attention to them. The closest of them is medicine, since in most lands there is found no Muslim physician whose testimony may be relied upon in matters in which the Law relies on the word of the physician, and none of the jurists desires to engage in it. Likewise enjoining the good and forbidding the evil, for it is one of the communal obligations. Often the debater, in his debating session, sees silk worn and spread out while he remains silent, and he debates a question that never happens to occur, and if it did occur, a group of jurists would take it up. Then he claims that he wants to draw near to Allah Most High through communal obligations.

Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that it was said, "O Messenger of Allah, when are enjoining the good and forbidding the evil abandoned?" He said (peace be upon him), "When flattery appears among the best of you, indecency among the worst of you, kingship passes to the youngest of you, and jurisprudence (fiqh) to the meanest of you." (١)

The third is that the debater be a mujtahid who gives legal opinions by his own judgment, not by the school of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, or others, so that if the truth becomes clear to him from the school of Abu Hanifa, he abandons what agrees with the view of al-Shafi'i and gives an opinion by what has become clear to him, as the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and the imams used to do.

As for one who does not have the rank of independent reasoning (ijtihad), which is the ruling for all the people of this age, he gives opinions only on what he is asked, transmitting from the school of its master. If the weakness of his school became clear to him, it would not be permissible for him to abandon it. So what benefit does he have in debate, when his school is known and he is not permitted to give opinions by another? And whatever is problematic for him, he must say: perhaps the master of my school has an answer to this, for I am not independent in exercising ijtihad regarding the foundation of the Law. And if his inquiry were about the questions in which his master has two views or two opinions, it would be more fitting, for he may give an opinion by one of them and gain from the inquiry an inclination to one of the two sides. But he does not see debates ever taking place on them; rather, he may even leave the question in which there are two views or two opinions and seek a question in which the disagreement is clear-cut.

The fourth is that he debates only in a question that has occurred or is likely to occur soon, for the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) consulted only on newly arisen events or what most likely occurs, like the shares of inheritance. Yet we do not see the debaters concerned with scrutinising the questions on which general need arises for a legal opinion; rather they seek the "drum" questions (tabuliyyat), which are heard of, so that the field of dispute in them widens however the matter may be.

Often they leave what occurs frequently, saying, "This is a report-based question," or "It is among the corners and not among the drum questions." It is among the wonders that the aim should be the truth, and then they leave the question because it is report-based and the means of attaining the truth in it is the report, or because it is not among the drums, so we do not lengthen the discussion on it.
What is intended in seeking the truth is that speech be kept short and reach the goal by the nearest way, not that it be lengthened.

The fifth is that debate in seclusion be dearer to him and more important than in gatherings and in the presence of the great and the sultans, for seclusion is more conducive to understanding and more apt for clarity of mind and thought and for grasping the truth, whereas the presence of a crowd stirs the motives of showing off (riya') and makes each one eager to support himself, whether in the right or in the wrong. And you know that their eagerness for gatherings and assemblies is not for Allah, and that one of them may be alone with his companion for a long time without speaking to him, and perhaps the companion proposes something to him and he does not answer; but when a prominent person appears or an assembly is formed, he leaves no resort of trickery untried until he alone is the one singled out for speaking.

The sixth is that in seeking the truth he be like one searching for something lost, who does not distinguish between whether the lost thing appears at his hand or at the hand of one who helps him; he sees his companion as a helper, not an adversary, and thanks him when he makes him aware of an error and shows him the truth, as if he took one road in search of what he lost and his companion alerted him to it on another road, in which case he would thank him and not blame him, honour him and be glad of him. Thus were the consultations of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), to the point that a woman objected to Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) and alerted him to the truth while he was delivering his sermon before a crowd of people, and he said, "A woman was right and a man was wrong."

A man asked Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and he answered him. The man said, "It is not so, O Commander of the Faithful, but it is such and such." He said, "You are right and I was wrong." ⟦QS 12:76⟧
Ibn Mas'ud corrected Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with them both), and Abu Musa said, "Do not ask me about anything while this learned man is among you."

That was when Abu Musa was asked about a man who fought in the cause of Allah and was killed, and he said, "He is in Paradise." He was the governor of Kufa. Ibn Mas'ud stood up and said, "Repeat it to the governor, perhaps he did not understand." They repeated it to him, and he repeated the answer. Ibn Mas'ud said, "And I say: if he is killed having hit upon the truth, he is in Paradise." Abu Musa said, "The truth is what he said." Such is fairness in seeking the truth. If something like this were mentioned today to the least of jurists, he would deny it and find it far-fetched, and say, "There is no need to say 'he hit upon the truth,' for that is known to everyone."

So look at the debaters of your time today: how the face of one of them turns black when the truth becomes clear on the tongue of his opponent, how he is ashamed because of it, how he strives with all his power to deny it, and how he disparages, throughout his life, the one who silenced him; then he is not ashamed to liken himself to the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) in their cooperation in examining the truth. The seventh is that he does not prevent his helper in the inquiry from moving from one proof to another and from one difficulty to another, for such were the debates of the early generations (salaf). And all the subtleties of innovated disputation, concerning what is for him and against him, fall away from his speech, such as his saying, "I am not obliged to mention this," and "This contradicts your first statement, so it is not accepted from you." For returning to the truth contradicts falsehood, and accepting it is obligatory.

And you see that all the sessions pass in parrying and wrangling, until the one offering proof draws an analogy from a root case on the basis of a cause ('illa) that he supposes, and it is said to him, "What is the evidence that the ruling in the root case is grounded in this cause?" and he says, "This is what has appeared to me; if something clearer and more fitting than it has appeared to you, mention it so that I may consider it."

Then the objector insists and says, "It has meanings besides what you mentioned. I know them and I will not mention them, since I am not obliged to mention them." The one offering proof says, "It is upon you to bring forward what you claim beyond this." And the objector insists that he is not obliged, and he aims, in debating sessions, at this kind of question and its like. This poor man does not know that his saying "I know it and I will not mention it since I am not obliged to" is a lie against the Law. For if he does not know its meaning and claims it only to leave his opponent helpless, he is a transgressor and a liar, has disobeyed Allah Most High and exposed himself to His wrath by claiming a knowledge of which he is empty; and if he is truthful, he has transgressed by concealing what he knew of the matter of the Law.

Yet his Muslim brother has asked him, so that he may make him understand and examine it: if it is strong, he returns to it, and if it is weak, he shows him its weakness and brings him out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge.
And there is no disagreement that revealing

what is known of the religious sciences, after being asked about it, is obligatory and binding. So the meaning of his saying "It is not binding on me" is: in the law of disputation that we have innovated, by virtue of whim and desire for the way of trickery and wrestling with words, it is not binding on me; otherwise it is binding by the Law, for by his refusal to mention it he is either a liar or a transgressor. So investigate the consultations of the Companions and the discussions of the early generations (salaf) (may Allah be pleased with them): did you hear in them anything resembling this kind? And was anyone prevented from moving from proof to proof, from analogy (qiyas) to a report (athar), and from a report (khabar) to a verse? Rather all their debates were of this kind, since they would mention whatever occurred to them as it occurred, and they would examine it.
The eighth is that he debates one from whom he expects to benefit, among those who are engaged in knowledge.

Mostly they guard against debating the eminent and the great, for fear of the truth appearing on their tongues, and so they incline toward those beneath them, hoping to pass falsehood off on them. Beyond these there are many subtle conditions, but in these eight conditions is what guides you to who debates for Allah and who debates for some ulterior motive.

In sum, know that whoever does not debate Satan, who has taken control of his heart and is his bitterest enemy and never ceases calling him to his destruction, and then busies himself debating others over questions in which the mujtahid is either right or shares with the one who is right in the reward, is the laughing stock of Satan and a lesson for the sincere. For that reason Satan gloats over him, since he has plunged him into the darkness of the afflictions that we enumerate and whose details we mention. So we ask Allah for good help and success.

independen.penilai: Agen pemeriksa-konten (claude-sonnet-5-5, konteks segar; penilaian AI, bukan manusia)

nilai.catatan: Judul bab lengkap dan setia.
Dalih para pendebat tetap milik mereka; daftar contoh dan nama ulama lengkap.
Delapan syarat; kalimat terpotong dibiarkan menggantung seperti sumber.
Makna terjaga, tetapi 'while he has not freed himself' menambah sambungan yang tidak ada di sumber.
Perumpamaan, pelaku, dan klaim 'mungkin terjadi' sesuai.
Kewajiban fardu ain, titip, dan syarat ketaatan (waktu, syarat, urutan) sesuai.
Syarat kedua, perumpamaan orang haus dan bekam, serta jawaban orang itu sesuai.
Fatwa sudah ada yang mengerjakan; tabib dan amar makruf; semua kalimat ada.
Perawi Anas, pertanyaan, sabda, dan penanda sesuai.
Syarat ketiga: mujtahid, bukan bermazhab; sesuai.
Muqallid tidak boleh meninggalkan mazhab; dua wajh atau dua qaul; sesuai.
Syarat keempat; para pendebat mengejar soal tabuliyyat; sesuai.
Setia, tetapi 'so we do not lengthen' tanpa tanda kutip bisa terbaca sebagai suara al-Ghazali, padahal itu alasan para pendebat.
Ringkas dan lengkap.
Syarat kelima; kontras khalwat dan majelis; lengkap.
Syarat keenam; perumpamaan barang hilang; ucapan Umar tetap miliknya.
'The man said' menambah subjek yang tidak tertulis di sumber; maknanya tepat tetapi tetap tambahan.
Ibn Mas'ud mengoreksi, Abu Musa berkata; pelaku tidak tertukar.
Makna benar, tetapi 'He was the governor of Kufa' tepat sesudah kutipan 'He is in Paradise' terbaca ganda.
Pelaku tiap kata kerja tepat; syarat ketujuh ada; ucapan pendebat tetap milik mereka.
Pemberi dalil dan penanya tidak tertukar; kalimat penutup lengkap.
Penolak dan pemberi dalil tidak tertukar; kedua cabang lengkap.
Kata ganti ambigu seperti di sumber; pembaca bisa menukar siapa yang memahamkan dan siapa yang menilai.
Awal kalimat terpotong dibiarkan menggantung seperti sumber.
Lanjutan lengkap; urutan qiyas, athar, khabar, ayat tepat.
Syarat kedelapan sesuai.
Pelaku 'mereka' dan delapan syarat sesuai.
Penutup lengkap: ditertawakan setan, dibenamkan dalam kegelapan, doa penutup ada.
